content:
Let a \(2\times2\) block be called **good** if it is chesslike. In a good block, the two cells on each of its diagonals have the same color.

**Upper bound.** Consider any NW-SE diagonal of the board. If three consecutive \(2\times2\) blocks along this diagonal were good, then their overlapping diagonal pairs would force four consecutive cells on that diagonal to have the same color, which is forbidden. Thus along each NW-SE diagonal, good blocks cannot occur in three consecutive positions.

A NW-SE diagonal with \(m\) adjacent pairs can therefore contain at most the maximum number of \(1\)'s in a length-\(m\) binary string with no \(111\), namely
\[
0,1,2,2,3,4,3,2,2,1,0
\]
for the diagonals with
\[
m=0,1,2,3,4,5,4,3,2,1,0.
\]
Summing gives
\[
0+1+2+2+3+4+3+2+2+1+0=20.
\]
So there are at most \(20\) chesslike squares.

**Construction.** Color the board as
\[
\begin{array}{cccccc}
R&G&R&R&G&R\\
G&R&G&G&R&G\\
R&G&R&R&G&R\\
G&R&G&G&R&G\\
R&G&R&R&G&R\\
G&R&G&G&R&G
\end{array}
\]
Each row has no run of length \(4\). Adjacent rows are complementary, so vertical runs are impossible. Every diagonal of length at least \(4\) has at most three consecutive equal colors.

For every adjacent pair of rows, all column pairs except columns \(3\)–\(4\) form chesslike \(2\times2\) blocks. The column pair \(3\)–\(4\) gives non-chesslike blocks in each of the \(5\) row pairs, so exactly \(5\) of the \(25\) blocks are not chesslike. Hence we get
\[
25-5=20
\]
chesslike squares.

Therefore the maximal possible number is \(\boxed{20}\).
